title: The Secure Shell (SSH) Authentication Protocol
organization: SSH Communications Security Corp; Cisco Systems, Inc.
subtitle: How an SSH server decides who you are, once the encrypted tunnel is up.
summary: RFC 4252 defines how an SSH client proves a user's identity to a server. The server drives the process by listing which authentication methods it will accept, and the client tries them in any order. The RFC specifies three methods: public key (required), password and host-based. It runs on top of the SSH transport layer, which supplies the encryption it depends on.

eli5.summary: Before the club lets you in, the doorkeeper tells you the ways you can prove who you are: show a secret stamp, say a password, or have a trusted friend vouch for you. You pick one, and the doorkeeper says yes or no.

questions: what does ssh msg userauth request contain

tldr.problem: After SSH has encrypted the connection and the client has verified the server, the server still has to find out which user is connecting.
tldr.mechanism: The client sends SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_REQUEST naming a user, a service and a method; the server answers with SUCCESS or with FAILURE plus the list of methods that may continue.
tldr.outcome: Public key authentication is mandatory and password is optional, so SSH logins can run without sending a reusable secret. This is still how SSH logins work.

today: This is the authentication step of essentially every SSH login. OpenSSH, the most widely deployed implementation, supports public key, password and host-based authentication as described here, and its authorized_keys file is the usual way a server decides whether a public key is acceptable for a user. Later RFCs refined the details: RFC 8332 added RSA signatures using SHA-2, and RFC 8308 added a way for client and server to negotiate extensions.

implementations.name: OpenSSH
implementations.note: The most widely used SSH client and server; implements publickey, password and hostbased authentication.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The SSH authentication protocol is a general-purpose user authentication protocol. It is meant to run over the SSH transport layer (RFC 4253) and assumes that layer already provides integrity and confidentiality. It should be read after the architecture document, RFC 4251, whose terminology it uses freely.

Its service name is "ssh-userauth". When it starts, it receives the session identifier from the layer below. That identifier is the exchange hash H from the first key exchange; it uniquely identifies the session and is suitable for signing, which is how a client proves it owns a private key. The protocol also needs to know whether the transport provides confidentiality.

Once authentication succeeds, the server starts the service the client asked for, typically the connection protocol in RFC 4254, which carries the terminal sessions and forwarded ports.

The transport layer has already authenticated the server to the client. This RFC is about the other direction: proving the user to the server.
sections.eli5: First the computer you are calling proves it is the real one, and the line is made private. Only then does it ask who you are. This RFC is the "who are you?" part.

sections.title: The authentication framework
sections.content:
The server drives authentication. At any moment it tells the client which methods can continue the exchange, and the client may try those methods in any order. That gives the server full control if it wants it, and lets the client pick whatever is most convenient.

The "none" method is reserved. The server must never list it as supported, but a client may send it, and the server must reject it unless that user really needs no authentication. Its main use is to make the server reveal its list of methods.

To limit abuse, a server should time out unauthenticated connections and cap failed attempts. The RECOMMENDED values are a 10 minute timeout and 20 failed attempts per session, after which the server should disconnect.

Server in charge
The server lists methods that may continue; the client chooses among them.
Method names
Defined names are publickey (REQUIRED), password (OPTIONAL), hostbased (OPTIONAL) and none (NOT RECOMMENDED).
Limits
Recommended: 10 minute timeout, 20 failed attempts.
sections.eli5: The doorkeeper decides which ways of proving yourself are allowed today, and you choose one from the list. If you keep getting it wrong or take too long, the doorkeeper sends you away.

sections.title: Requests and responses
sections.content:
Every attempt is a SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_REQUEST (message 50) carrying a user name in UTF-8, a service name in US-ASCII, a method name in US-ASCII, then fields that depend on the method. The user name and service name are repeated in every attempt and may change; the server must check them each time and discard any partial authentication state if they change, or disconnect if it cannot.

If a request fails, the server replies SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_FAILURE (51) with a name-list of methods that can continue and a boolean partial success. Partial success is TRUE if the request itself succeeded but more authentication is needed, and FALSE otherwise. When authentication is complete the server sends SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_SUCCESS (52), exactly once; it is not sent after each step of a multi-method login.

A server may also send SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_BANNER (53) at any time before success, containing text such as a legal warning for the client to display. If the user name does not exist, the server may disconnect or send a bogus method list, but must never accept, so account names are not revealed.

All authentication messages fall in the range 50 to 79. Messages numbered 80 and higher belong to the service that runs afterwards, so receiving one before authentication is complete is an error and the server must disconnect.
sections.eli5: You hand over a card saying who you are and how you will prove it. The doorkeeper answers "come in", or "not that way, try these instead". Sometimes the doorkeeper wants two proofs, and says "good so far, one more".

sections.title: Public key authentication
sections.content:
The "publickey" method is the only REQUIRED one; every implementation must support it. Possession of a private key is the proof: the client sends a signature made with the user's private key, and the server checks both that the key is valid for that user and that the signature is correct.

Because private keys are often passphrase-protected and signing is expensive, the client may first send a query request with the boolean set to FALSE, naming an algorithm and a public key blob. The server answers SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_PK_OK (60) if it would accept that key, or FAILURE. The client may skip the query and send the signature directly.

The real request has the boolean TRUE and ends with a signature. The signed data is the session identifier, then the request fields (message number, user name, service name, "publickey", TRUE, algorithm name, public key). Because the session identifier is included, a signature captured from one session cannot be replayed in another.
sections.eli5: You own a special pen that nobody else has. You first ask "would you accept my pen?". When the doorkeeper says yes, you sign a note that includes today's secret session number and hand it over. The doorkeeper checks your signature against the pen on file.

sections.title: Password authentication
sections.content:
The "password" method is OPTIONAL, though all implementations SHOULD support it. The request carries a boolean FALSE and the plaintext password in UTF-8. A client that reads the password in another encoding must convert it, and systems with non-ASCII passwords should normalize them, using SASLprep (RFC 4013) where they both store and compare passwords.

The password is sent in clear inside the packet, but the whole packet is encrypted by the transport layer. Both sides should therefore check that confidentiality is actually in effect: if the "none" cipher is in use, password authentication SHOULD be disabled, and if there is no confidentiality or no MAC, password change SHOULD be disabled.

If the password has expired, the server answers SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_PASSWD_CHANGEREQ (60) with a prompt and language tag, and must never let the expired password authenticate. The client may then retry with a request whose boolean is TRUE, carrying both the old and the new password.
sections.eli5: You whisper your secret word to the doorkeeper through a tube nobody else can hear into. If the word is too old, the doorkeeper asks you to pick a new one.

sections.title: Host-based authentication
sections.content:
The "hostbased" method is OPTIONAL and, the RFC says, "not suitable for high-security sites" even though it can be very convenient. It resembles the Unix rhosts and hosts.equiv styles of trust, but the client host's identity is checked cryptographically rather than by address.

The client sends the host key algorithm, the client host's public key (possibly with certificates), the client host name as an FQDN, the user name on the client host, and a signature made with the host's private key. The signed data is the session identifier plus those same fields. The server must verify that the key belongs to the named host, that the given user on that host is allowed in, and that the signature is valid. It may ignore the client user name if it wants to authenticate only the host.

Special care SHOULD be taken to stop ordinary users from obtaining the private host key, since anyone who has it can vouch for any user on that host. Servers are also advised to check that the network address matches the claimed host name.
sections.eli5: Instead of proving who you are yourself, a trusted friend's computer stands up and says "I vouch for this person", and signs it. This is only as safe as the friend's signature stays secret.

sections.title: Security considerations
sections.content:
This section of the RFC is short because the protocol deliberately leaves most of the security work to the layer below. It assumes the transport has already authenticated the server machine, set up an encrypted channel, and computed a unique session identifier. The transport layer provides forward secrecy for password authentication and other methods that rely on secret data.

The full security considerations are in the architecture document, RFC 4251. Several rules in this RFC are security measures in themselves: signatures bind to the session identifier, servers must not reveal which accounts exist, authentication attempts are limited by timeout and count, and banner text should be filtered for terminal control characters to avoid attacks that send them.
sections.eli5: The doorkeeper only works safely because the phone line was already made private and you already know you called the right place. If that were not true, nothing here would help.

cells: Signature with the user's private key
Plaintext password, protected by the transport encryption
Signature with the client host's private key, plus user and host names
Nothing; used to ask the server for its method list

data.title: Authentication messages (RFC 4252 notation)
data.code:
byte      SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_REQUEST   (50)
string    user name (UTF-8)
string    service name (US-ASCII)
string    method name (US-ASCII)
....      method specific fields

byte      SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_FAILURE   (51)
name-list authentications that can continue
boolean   partial success

byte      SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_SUCCESS   (52)

byte      SSH_MSG_USERAUTH_BANNER    (53)
string    message (UTF-8)
string    language tag

viz.caption: Public key login with a key query

messages.label: USERAUTH_FAILURE (publickey,password)
messages.note: Methods that can continue; partial success FALSE.

messages.label: USERAUTH_REQUEST "publickey", FALSE, algorithm, key
messages.note: Optional query: would this key be acceptable?

messages.label: USERAUTH_REQUEST "publickey", TRUE, ..., signature
messages.note: Signature covers the session identifier and request fields.

items.title: Sent inside encryption
items.text: The plaintext password is protected only by the transport layer, so password authentication should be disabled with the "none" cipher.

items.title: UTF-8 and normalization
items.text: Clients convert to UTF-8; systems with non-ASCII passwords should normalize, using RFC 4013.

items.title: Expired passwords
items.text: The server replies PASSWD_CHANGEREQ (60) and never accepts the expired password.

items.title: Changing needs integrity
items.text: With no confidentiality or no MAC, password change should be disabled.
